title: Enhanced Coulomb pseudopotentials in high-pressure hydrides from first principles
abstract: In the Eliashberg theory of superconductivity, Coulomb interactions oppose the phonon-mediated attraction and suppress the superconducting critical temperature $T_{\mathrm{c}}$. However, most first-principles predictions continue to treat this repulsion with an empirical Coulomb pseudopotential $\mu^*_{\text{ME}}$ in the range 0.1-0.15. Here we present first-principles calculations of the Coulomb parameter $\mu$ and pseudopotential $\mu^*_{\text{ME}}$ in superconducting hydrides across a range of pressures. The screened Coulomb interaction is evaluated at the random phase approximation level with the Mantel code. We demonstrate that several hydride systems, including H$_3$S, YSbH$_6$ and Mg$_2$IrH$_6$, have strong Coulomb repulsions driven by a large density of states at the Fermi energy, $N_{\mathrm{F}}$. For Mg$_2$IrH$_6$ we obtain $\mu=0.62$ and $\mu^*_{\text{ME}}\approx0.39$, leading to a 40 K suppression in $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ relative to a standard $\mu^*_{\text{ME}}=0.16$. Our obtained $\mu^*_{\text{ME}}$ is far above the conventional range and, accounting for the energy dependence of the density of states, resolves the factor-of-two discrepancy between $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ estimates of previous studies. Across all systems and pressures studied, we find that $\mu$ closely tracks $N_{\mathrm{F}}$, suggesting that commonly used $\mu^*_{\text{ME}}$ values lead to overestimated $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ in materials where the density of states at the Fermi energy is large.

title: Parallel Design of a GPU-Resident Semi-Lagrangian Drift-Kinetic Solver on Unstructured Extruded Tokamak Meshes
abstract: Semi-Lagrangian (SL) schemes advect a distribution function along characteristics and remap it to a fixed grid. They are unconditionally stable without a global solve, and with discontinuous Galerkin (DG) integration the transfer along a magnetic field line conserves mass exactly. This paper presents the parallel and GPU design of a 3X+2V SLDG drift-kinetic tokamak solver on unstructured, flux-surface-aligned poloidal planes of shaped cross section, extruded toroidally. Transport follows magnetic field lines across the planes, and each velocity channel advances a fixed distance per step, proportional to its parallel speed, so the halo depth a channel needs grows with its speed. Velocity-dependent ragged halos exploit this, sending each channel only its own upwind depth. The 4D decomposition includes the toroidal angle, the 2D poloidal plane and the magnetic moment, and leaves the parallel velocity whole: no stage transports across the magnetic moment, while a parallel-velocity partition would put a halo inside the acceleration stage. On NVIDIA A100s the design strong-scales over the magnetic-moment axis from one to 12 four-GPU nodes, and a weak series of three points refining all five phase-space dimensions together, 16x in total per series point, holds a weak-scaling efficiency of 75% on 16 GPUs and 57% on 256, from a one-GPU base case. The pointwise interpolations within the poloidal plane do not conserve mass, and the full step's mass drift stays below 2.1x10^-5 at every series point. The design was implemented with an AI code assistant under a machine-checked regression discipline, in which every change is held to one of four exactness classes, from bit-identical to a physics rate within a stated tolerance.

title: Fourier Transform-Based Computation of Two-Electron Four-Center Coulomb Repulsion Integrals
abstract: We present a Fourier-based method for evaluating two-electron four-center Coulomb repulsion integrals over Slater-type orbitals. Spherical Fourier-Bessel coefficients of the convolution factors are precomputed and reused. Since the spherical part of the integral can be evaluated directly, there remains only a one-dimensional quadrature problem in the radial direction. For the ten reference integrals reported here, the largest absolute discrepancy is $1.7\times10^{-9}$. A preliminary resident-cache benchmark computes approximately $4.2\times10^5$ unique integrals per second on an NVIDIA V100 at the contraction stage.

title: Evaluating LLMs for Translating Legacy Fortran Atmospheric Physics to GPU-Accelerated JAX
abstract: Legacy Fortran physics packages in atmospheric models such as CESM, WRF, and E3SM pose a barrier to GPU modernization, while manual porting requires accelerator-programming expertise. We present LAFT (LLM-Assisted Fortran Translation), an agentic framework for converting Fortran atmospheric physics parameterizations into GPU-accelerated JAX while preserving numerical agreement with the Fortran reference. LAFT coordinates source-code analysis, translation, repair, runtime validation, and performance profiling. It combines a deterministic front end for metadata extraction and bridge generation, structured translation prompts, numerical validation, and profiling-guided feedback to identify inefficient execution patterns. The bridge handles array-layout conversion separately from scientific computation. We evaluate LAFT using the Kessler warm-rain microphysics scheme and four LLMs: Claude, GPT, Gemini, and Qwen. All four validated translations reproduce the Fortran reference outputs to near floating-point precision for the evaluated case, but their GPU performance differs substantially with execution design. The Gemini-generated implementation achieves up to a 357-fold speedup over serial Fortran in cached execution at 1,000,000 atmospheric columns, excluding compilation and host-device transfers. The results demonstrate that numerical agreement alone does not ensure efficient GPU execution and motivate combining numerical validation with hardware-aware performance analysis. LAFT provides a practical workflow for modernizing legacy atmospheric physics code through LLM-assisted translation, deterministic interface generation, automated validation and repair, and reproducible profiling.

title: Homogeneous to multi-scale inhomogeneous complex magnetism in Ba3LnRu2O9 (Ln = Gd, Ho), Revealed by muSR and Machine-Learned Muon-Site Calculations
abstract: We report a comprehensive muon spin rotation and relaxation (muSR) study of the hexagonal 6H-perovskites Ba3LnRu2O9 (Ln = Gd, Ho) to investigate the role of rare-earth anisotropy in the magnetic ground state of 4d-4f coupled systems. Ba3HoRu2O9 exhibits two successive magnetic orderings at TN1 = 46 K and TN2 = 10 K, leading to a complex magnetic ground state, whereas Ba3GdRu2O9, with Gd3+ (L = 0) S-state ions, shows primarily single magnetic ordering at TN = 14.5 K. Zero-field (ZF) and longitudinal-field (LF) muSR measurements reveal markedly different magnetic behavior despite their structural similarity. Ba3HoRu2O9 displays a multi-scale inhomogeneous magnetic state characterized by two-component exponential relaxation, broad local-field distributions, incomplete LF decoupling, and persistent spin dynamics. The muSR results identify two characteristic magnetic energy scales near 46 and 10 K, associated with correlated Ru-Ho interactions and quasistatic magnetic ordering, respectively. Redfield analysis further demonstrates strong local magnetic fields and distributed spin fluctuation timescales, confirming magnetic inhomogeneity. Machine-learning-assisted muon-site and dipolar-field calculations show that the broad field distribution naturally arises from muons sensing distinct coexisting magnetic domains at different structural sites. In contrast, Ba3GdRu2O9 exhibits a comparatively homogeneous antiferromagnetic ground state below 14.5 K, with Gaussian relaxation consistent with a narrow static field distribution. These results establish that the rare-earth ion in Ba3LnRu2O9 is a powerful tuning parameter, driving the ground state from homogeneous to complex, multi-scale inhomogeneous behavior through competing 4d-4f magnetic interactions.

title: Polyconvex neural-network surrogates with learned paired directional features for anisotropic hyperelastic homogenization
abstract: Approximating the effective anisotropic hyperelastic response of a representative volume element (RVE) requires constitutive expressiveness, mechanical consistency, and computational efficiency. This work develops a polyconvex physics-augmented neural network (PANN) construction based on paired directional features whose orientations, stretch powers, and determinant exponents adapt to the RVE response. The features are composed with convex, componentwise nondecreasing cores, realized as an input-convex neural network (ICNN) or an input-convex Kolmogorov-Arnold network (ICKAN). The complete energies satisfy objectivity, an exactly stress-free reference, two-dimensional polyconvexity, and prescribed growth conditions by construction, and nonnegative energy is certified separately for the selected models. On a multicavity and a single-cavity periodic cell, these energies are compared with an Unconstrained energy, trained identically without the curvature and growth constraints, and with three hyperreduced projection-based reduced-order models (HPROMs), which serve as physics-based references. On the first cell, learning the features lowers the stress error sevenfold, and six features suffice on both. The constrained energies remain below one percent in stress error and in the displacement error of a tensile-coupon FE$^2$ application with a full-order reference, whereas the Unconstrained energy and the HPROMs are more accurate inside the data. Beyond the data, however, the Unconstrained energy loses rank-one convexity, and under confined compression it stops below half of the 500 MPa that the constrained energies reach. These results quantify what the guarantees cost in accuracy and what they secure beyond the data.

title: Riemannian Hessian analysis of Sobolev gradient flows for the Gross--Pitaevskii ground state problem
abstract: Sobolev gradient flows for the Gross--Pitaevskii ground state problem are Riemannian gradient descent methods on the sphere under a metric induced by a discrete elliptic operator. We analyze their convergence through the condition number of the Riemannian Hessian at the ground state. Bounds of the Rayleigh quotient of the Riemannian Hessian give a uniform analysis of these methods for different metrics. The uniform analysis applies to the classical metrics, such as the shifted Laplacian and the energy-adaptive metrics. Inspired by this analysis, we also consider three new metrics. One of them is a Thomas--Fermi metric, whose condition number is bounded uniformly in the interaction strength for the one-dimensional harmonic trap and whose iteration count does not grow in the Thomas--Fermi regime in the numerical tests. The performance suggested by our analysis is consistent with three-dimensional numerical tests with up to one billion unknowns, for both Riemannian gradient descent and Riemannian conjugate gradient methods, whose practical performance is also related to the Hessian condition number. The Thomas--Fermi flow needs the fewest iterations, while the metrics inverted exactly by tensor-product solvers are the fastest in computational time on one GPU card.

title: All-electron RT-TDDFT with Exact Exchange based on Numeric Atom-centered Orbitals for Condensed Matter
abstract: Real-time time-dependent density functional theory (RT-TDDFT) has become a widely used first-principles method for studying excited-state and nonequilibrium electron dynamics. Hybrid exchange-correlation (XC) functionals, which incorporate a fraction of nonlocal exact exchange, are particularly important for accurately describing processes such as charge transfer and hot-carrier dynamics. However, the high computational cost which accompanies exact exchange, as required in hybrid XC functionals, has largely restricted RT-TDDFT simulations of condensed matter systems to using semi-local XC functionals. In this work, we present an all-electron implementation of exact exchange for RT-TDDFT based on numeric atom-centered orbitals, extending an efficient ground-state resolution-of-identity (RI) framework to the complex, time-dependent Hamiltonians required for real-time propagation. We validate the implementation against an established RI approach, for an isolated water molecule, finding exact agreement for both valence and core (K-edge) excitations. We also demonstrate the method on two extended periodic systems, crystalline silicon and silicon carbide. For silicon, the HSE06 spectrum reproduces previously reported real-time TDDFT results and agrees with experiment to within approximately 0.2~eV, consistent with plane-wave pseudopotential implementations. For silicon carbide, we compute valence and X-ray absorption spectra at the silicon $L$-edge and carbon $K$-edge. These results establish an efficient, all-electron route to hybrid-XC functional RT-TDDFT for both molecular and condensed matter systems.

title: Alter-excitons in Altermagnets: Symmetry, Splitting and Dispersion
abstract: Magnetism provides a fertile platform for discovering emergent quantum phenomena governed by symmetry. Recent developments of spin-space-group (SSG) theory have revealed altermagnets as a distinct class of nonrelativistic collinear magnets with unconventional spin-dependent electronic structures. Here, we demonstrate that altermagnetic symmetry imposes fundamentally different constraints on electronic and excitonic excitations. Although the quasiparticle and two-body Hamiltonians possess identical SSG symmetries, we find that symmetry-protected degeneracies present in the electronic band structure can be intrinsically lifted in the exciton spectrum at specific momenta. This splitting arises solely from the many-body nature of excitons and does not require spin-orbit coupling or noncollinear magnetic order. Combining symmetry analysis with many-body perturbation theory, we predict a novel class of spin-split excitonic quasiparticles, termed alter-excitons, and reveal their characteristic dispersions in altermagnetic systems. Our results establish excitons as a sensitive probe of hidden spin-space symmetries and uncover a new route toward symmetry-engineered many-body phenomena in collinear magnets.

title: Low-Rank Kolmogorov-Arnold Generator Flows for Interpretable Operator Learning
abstract: Neural operators that learn physical laws from data should generalize beyond their training distribution and expose the learned law in closed form. The Kolmogorov-Arnold neural operator achieves both for position-dependent dynamics by learning a dense pseudo-differential symbol over all positions and frequencies, at a cost that grows with the square of the resolution and with closed forms that must be read out by hand. This dense symbol is unnecessary: a finite-order variable-coefficient differential operator has a symbol whose separation rank is bounded by the number of its coefficient functions, independently of the resolution, and the symbols that this network learns on its own benchmarks have rank two. We introduce the Kolmogorov-Arnold flow (KAFlow), which learns the generator of a physical operator as a low-rank symbol built from univariate Kolmogorov-Arnold functions, fixes the gauge of these functions so that every term has a unique place, integrates the dynamics with exact exponential integrators, and distills its closed form automatically. On the synthetic benchmarks of the Kolmogorov-Arnold neural operator, KAFlow lowers the out-of-distribution loss by 3.4 to 11 times and recovers every coefficient to within 10^-4 without symbolic templates, reaching the precision floor of the data. On long-horizon quantum dynamics, it lowers the state infidelity by up to 6 orders of magnitude, and by 30 times when trained only on position and momentum measurements. KAFlow also learns a variable-order fractional operator 15 times more accurately than existing operator networks and discovers nonlocal, fractional and non-polynomial dispersion relations on which sparse regression fails.

title: Ultrafast laser-stimulated field emission from a metal: a non-equilibrium Green's functions approach
abstract: Ultrafast laser-assisted field emission from metallic nanotips is a promising route for generating coherent electron pulses. However, existing theoretical models often neglect many-body strong correlation effects in the emitter's electronic structure and its response to the optical field. In this work, we propose a theoretical framework based on the non-equilibrium Green's function formalism to simulate the out-of-equilibrium electron dynamics across a strongly driven matter-vacuum interface, in a one-dimensional model. Treating the tip-vacuum coupling perturbatively, we find that the interplay between strong-field emission and multi-photon emission regimes can be described in terms of a filtering of the emitter's local density of occupied states through field-dressed vacuum propagators. By including electron-electron interactions via the second-Born approximation, we show that correlation-induced modifications in the electronic structure are directly transferred to the far-field spectrum. Finally, by self-consistently solving the Dyson equation at the interface, we uncover a dynamic back-action regime driven by the optical field, characterized by a periodic polarization of the emitter, which reshapes the far-field spectrum. This shows that the non-equilibrium Green's functions approach provides a versatile framework for exploring and analyzing field emission of correlated electrons.

title: Recovering Irreducible Three-Body Interactions with Lagrangian Neural Networks
abstract: Lagrangian Neural Networks (LNNs) learn mechanical systems from trajectory data by parameterizing a scalar Lagrangian and deriving the dynamics through the Euler-Lagrange equations, biasing the model toward motion that respects the variational structure of mechanics. The interactions studied so far have been pairwise-additive, leaving open whether LNNs can recover an irreducible many-body interaction from motion alone. We address this using the Axilrod-Teller triple-dipole interaction, the leading three-body dispersion term, whose dependence on the collective geometry of three particles cannot be represented by any sum of pairwise terms. We prescribe the kinetic energy exactly and learn only the potential, as a function of interparticle distances and angles. Combined with a signal-aware sampling strategy that concentrates training data where the three-body signal is strongest while preserving broad coverage of configuration space, this recovers the interaction from accelerations alone. The learned potential reproduces the radial scaling, angular dependence, and characteristic sign reversal of the Axilrod-Teller interaction, and generates stable trajectories. Embedding it within a pairwise Lennard-Jones potential lets us examine its observability: the three-body term is recovered once its dynamical signature exceeds the residual modeling error, which it does cleanly at amplified coupling but not at the coupling of a real noble gas, bracketing the transition between the two. Finally, symbolic regression on the trained potential, with no assumed functional form, returns the Axilrod-Teller expression with angular numerator, radial law, and coupling constant intact. An LNN with domain-specific structure can thus recover an irreducible three-body interaction from trajectories as a closed-form law, pointing toward learning interaction laws whose structure is not known a priori.

title: Global Optimization of Beam Profiles for Suppressing the Bump-On-Tail Instability
abstract: A particle beam with constant intensity that propagates into a plasma triggers a bump-on-tail instability. It has been demonstrated that beam modulation can be used to significantly reduce this instability. However, finding the optimal beam profiles that accomplish this is a complex optimization problem that suffers from an extremely rugged optimization landscape and a relatively high-dimensional parameter space. In this paper, we evaluate a number of optimization algorithms and find that population based methods (in particular, CMA-ES and Differential Evolution) perform best. In particular, we investigate beam profiles where the beam is either completely turned ON or OFF. This configuration is easier to accomplish experimentally, but leads to a higher-dimensional and thus more challenging optimization problem. We obtain ON/OFF beam profiles that reduce the instability by more than 80% and thus perform significantly better than what has been reported in the literature.

title: VN-GraphGG: von Neumann--Mullins--based graph grain growth simulation
abstract: Efficient simulations of grain growth are essential for investigating the process-structure-property relationships in polycrystalline materials. We introduce a two-dimensional von Neumann-Mullins-based graph grain growth simulation (VN-GraphGG), which couples the grain-scale kinetics with microstructure reconstruction. The polycrystalline microstructure is represented as a graph with grain and junction nodes. The grain-area evolution on the grain graph is governed by the von Neumann--Mullins (VN) law, while a graph neural network is trained to reconstruct the microstructure from the graph. This separation allows kinetic coefficients to be varied without retraining the neural reconstruction model. Topological changes during grain growth such as disappearance of grains and changes in neighbor relations are handled straightforwardly through reconstruction and postprocessing. Simulations demonstrate accurate predictions of VN kinetics and coarsening statistics, and significant speedup over the phase-field simulations. The proposed method provides a foundation for efficient grain growth simulation based on grain-scale kinetics, opening the way to incorporate a broader range of physical mechanisms. An application example is presented for abnormal grain growth, in which kinetic heterogeneity significantly influences the grain microstructure evolution.

title: Predicting Nanofabrication Variance: A Conditional Diffusion Model
abstract: Micro- and nanostructures fabricated by focused ion beam (FIB) milling invariably deviate from input designs due to systematic and stochastic effects such as ablation-rate fluctuations, and redeposition. As such, nominally identical iterations of a given process yield a distribution of non-identical fabrication outcomes, leading to variations in the physical (optical, mechanical) properties of fabricated structures. Existing models of the milling process typically predict a single deterministic fabrication result, neglecting this variability. Here we present a conditional diffusion model that learns the statistical distribution of process outcomes conditioned on input design, enabling it to predict a realistic distribution of possible output sample structures. These predictions accurately reproduce edge morphology, linewidth variations, and defect probabilities observed in fabricated samples, enabling statistical analysis of milling performance and the identification of dominant structural and process parameter-dependent deformation modes. The work establishes a probabilistic modelling framework for fabrication variability analysis and fabrication-aware design optimization.

title: Implementation and verification of a new free boundary module for Resistive Wall Modes simulations with the nonlinear 3D full MHD code SpeCyl
abstract: Self-consistent numerical simulations of free boundary instabilities, such as resistive wall modes (RWMs) and external kink modes, require special attention given their relevance on the path towards magnetic fusion based nuclear reactors. In this work, a new implementation and a verification benchmark are presented for the nonlinear three-dimensional (3D) full magneto-hydrodynamics (MHD) code SpeCyl, which self-consistently combines a free flow 3D treatment for the edge plasma velocity with double resistive wall thin shell magnetic boundary conditions, capable of capturing the essential features of common setups in experimental devices. Two coaxial resistive shells surround the plasma. Vacuum conditions are assumed between and outside the resistive shells, whose relative positions and time constants can be varied on purpose. The implementation is extensively verified against Shafranov's analytic theory, valid for a circular cross section large aspect ratio tokamak and assuming a flat current profile. The correctness of newly implemented Boundary Conditions (BCs) is confirmed by the good agreement obtained for the linear growth rates of (m=2,n=1) RWM and external kink, over a wide range of wall positions, resistive shell time constants, and for different initial reference equilibria. The (m=2,n=1) RWM growth rates are also benchmarked against previous different RWMs modelling and successful validation studies for RFX-mod tokamak plasmas. The new BCs make SpeCyl a flexible and robust tool to investigate free boundary MHD modes in large aspect ratio magnetic confinement configurations, such as those achieved with the RFX-mod machine and expected in RFX-mod2.

title: Energy-dependent trapping of backscattered helium during magnetron sputtering growth: A molecular dynamics study
abstract: Helium incorporation during magnetron sputtering can strongly affect thin film growth and lead to the formation of gas/solid nanocomposites and nanoporous structures. Here, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations are used to investigate the trapping mechanism of helium atoms (He) and the subsequent formation of He bubbles during the sputter deposition of aluminum (Al) and titanium (Ti) thin films. The simulations account for the kinetic energy distributions of sputtered metal atoms and backscattered gas species. Results indicate that He is efficiently incorporated into the growing films, leading to the formation of high-pressure, dense He bubbles, with a much higher He-to-metal atomic ratio in Ti ($\sim$ 60%) than in Al ($\sim$ 12%). More importantly, the simulations reveal a clear energy dependence of He trapping in Ti: background He atoms at thermal energies are essentially not incorporated, whereas efficient trapping starts at an incident energy of approximately 20 eV and increases up to a saturation regime near 100 eV. Simulated thermal desorption spectroscopy (TDS) further reveals distinct release mechanisms in the two investigated metals: He desorption from Al occurs at higher temperatures and is preceded by the removal of surface Al atoms, whereas He and Ti atom desorption starts continuously around 950 K, leading to a porous structure. Comparative simulations with argon (Ar) demonstrate negligible trapping even at comparable kinetic energy or momentum, showing that neither parameter alone accounts for the strong He incorporation observed in Ti. The above results are in very good agreement with what is reported in literature for low-kinetic energy He ion implantation in metal surfaces, suggesting similar insertion mechanisms. They clarify the atomistic conditions governing noble gas trapping during film growth and provide a basis for controlling He incorporation and porosity in films synthesized by magnetron sputtering.

title: Encoding Matters: A Qubit-Efficient Reformulation for Quantum Resilient Routing
abstract: Qubits are powerful computational resources because each additional qubit doubles the size of the accessible state space. This expressive power comes at a cost: adding qubits also increases circuit size, constraint overhead, and exposure to hardware noise. These limitations are especially critical for near-term quantum computers, making the number of qubits required to formulate a problem a central practical concern. In this work, we present a method for efficiently mapping logistics and routing problems onto qubits through structure-aware encoding reduction. We demonstrate the method on a benchmark problem of latency-resilient routing under dual-link failures. For this benchmark, the reduced formulation substantially lowers both the qubit count and the compiled circuit complexity while preserving the original optimization task. By running the reduced model on the same trapped-ion quantum computer as the benchmark, we obtain a 100X improvement in the success probability. This finding shows how careful problem formulation can make current quantum hardware substantially more effective for practical optimization.

title: Physical-state supervision for design-only Gaussian process surrogates of implosion simulations
abstract: Physical diagnostics recorded during simulation can organize a sharply varying response, but using them as surrogate inputs normally requires another calculation at prediction. We construct a physical-state-supervised Gaussian process surrogate that learns these diagnostics from design variables. Cross-fitted state estimates augment a retained design representation; a global Gaussian process and an optional soft mixture of response-band experts use identical inputs. On a database of 1,987 paired one-dimensional implosions, learned burn-weighted states from calculations without alpha-particle heating reduce mean squared log-response error by 60.25% and 52.98% for the global predictor on random holdout and design-space extrapolation. Random-projection and shuffled-state supervision do not reproduce these gains. For CH, matched-input comparisons show that experts help at smaller training budgets but contribute little at 1,000 designs with this representation. A thermal-feedback benchmark validates the complete learned-state procedure, while 3,000 newly calculated Be/Cocktail designs expose weaker extrapolation gains and cases where experts degrade accuracy. A conditional state-error bound separates encoding sensitivity from routing effects. An open Python implementation reproduces the archived predictions and is released with the data, per-design results, and measured costs. Physical-state supervision is thus a useful representation for finite-data surrogates, whereas expert specialization should be selected by validation.

title: Final-state centrality in relativistic heavy-ion simulations from neural networks
abstract: Experiments in relativistic heavy-ion collisions determine centrality from final-state quantities, usually the charged-particle multiplicity. Performing the same in hydrodynamic simulations requires millions of events, which is impractical for state-of-the-art hybrid models, and centrality is therefore commonly approximated by the initial entropy or energy. We show that neural networks trained on a few hundred hybrid events predict the event-by-event multiplicity and mean transverse momentum $[p_T]$ with relative errors of 1--2\%, which makes it possible to generate millions of collisions at a small fraction of the cost of the full simulation. For Pb--Pb collisions at $2.76$~TeV and Au--Au collisions at $200$~GeV, the initial-state and final-state definitions select nearly the same events in 10\%-wide classes, but up to 20\% of the events change class when the classes are 1\% wide. We then compute the fluctuations of $[p_T]$ and its Pearson correlations with a proxy of the elliptic flow, estimated from the initial eccentricity, and with multiplicity. The first correlation is insensitive to how centrality is defined, while the second changes substantially. The approach can be applied at every design point of Bayesian analyses at modest additional cost.
